newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Izetbegovic warns of warfare if accords not honored.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic warns of warfare if accords not honored.

text.p: Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic warned on Tuesday that war could break out again if the United States and others continued to ignore violations of the 1995 Balkan peace agreements.
He said the West should stop congratulating itself on fulfilling the military aspects of the accords, initialed in Dayton, Ohio, that resulted in NATO-led forces in Bosnia.

"I feel free to state that this is not all that much," he said in a speech. "If the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement are not implemented, its military results will be null as if they never even were. We could again have war.
"If the negative trend is not halted, the Dayton agreement will end and the situation will be out of control," he said.

Izetbegovic spoke after he received an award from the Washington-based Centre for Democracy, a private group that promotes democratic institutions abroad. He met U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen in Washington on Monday.

Cohen opposes a bill introduced in the House of Representatives last week calling for the withdrawal of U.S. ground troops from Bosnia by the end of 1997 rather than June 1998 as the Clinton administration plans.

Izetbegovic also chastised an unnamed U.S. official for saying U.S. soldiers would withdraw from Bosnia within a pre-determined time, believing that if Bosnians, Serbs and Croats wanted to fight it was their choice.
"Is it really about the warring parties wanting to fight and are there not other reasons on the scene that could lead to restarting the war?" he asked.

Izetbegovic said the world had turned a blind eye to clear violations of the 1995 peace agreement, particularly by the Serbs based in Pale, Bosnia. He did not, however, mention any violations by the Bosnian Croats.

"There is no freedom of movement, no return of refugees and the Pale regime publicly states that it will not deliver war criminals and that it will not accept the Central Bank and common currency, all of which they are obligated to do by the peace agreement," he said.
"For this there have been no adequate reactions," he said.
The Dayton agreement, he said, was a delicate balance of various interests and the Serbs could not implement only the parts that suited them.

Instead, he said, the world should "stop with the policy of yielding to evil and injustice because that only encourages the extremists, and do not say that all are equally guilty because this is historically untrue."

He said the time for negotiations had passed and nations should demand the accord be fulfilled. They should "force all the parties to adjust their constitutions" with the Dayton agreement and destroy all surplus arms. He said war criminals should be punished and a free press instituted.
"We know that the great part of the job we should do by ourselves, for this is all about our country. But in the situation as it is, we need your help," he said.
